Title: The Sun Never Set (Part 4 of 10): Losing America, Gaining the World, 1783–1815

Summary: After losing the thirteen colonies, Britain did not shrink. It turned to India, founded a penal colony in Australia, took the Cape and Ceylon, fought Revolutionary and Napoleonic France for over twenty years, crushed rebellions in Ireland and the Caribbean, and abolished its own slave trade. This post covers 1783 to 1815 and shows how the Haitian Revolution, the Irish rising of 1798 and the fall of Tipu Sultan fit together.

---

## The big picture

Historians used to talk about a "first" British Empire in the Atlantic, which ended in 1783, and a "second" one centred on Asia. That division is too neat, since the Caribbean and Canada stayed British, but the shift was real. In 1783 Britain ruled a small part of India. By 1815 it controlled most of it, plus key naval bases from the Cape to Malta to Ceylon, and the beginnings of Australia.

All of this happened during the longest war in modern British history. Britain was at war with France almost without a break from 1793 to 1815.

## Main timeline (1783–1800)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1783–1784 | Around 60,000 Loyalists leave the United States, many to Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Quebec | They help create English-speaking Canada; Black Loyalists are among them |
| 1784 | Pitt's India Act creates a Board of Control in London | Shared rule between the Company and the government |
| 1786 | Penang acquired by the EIC | First British base in the Malay world |
| 1787 | "Province of Freedom" settlement at Sierra Leone for Black Londoners; Society for Effecting the Abolition of the Slave Trade founded | The abolition movement becomes organised |
| 1788 | **First Fleet arrives at Botany Bay and Sydney Cove (January)**; impeachment trial of Warren Hastings begins | Australia is founded as a penal colony on land claimed as unowned |
| 1790–1792 | Third Anglo-Mysore War | Tipu Sultan loses half his territory |
| 1791 | Constitutional Act splits Quebec into Upper and Lower Canada | |
| 1792 | Freetown founded by about 1,200 Black Loyalists from Nova Scotia | |
| 1793 | War with Revolutionary France; Permanent Settlement in Bengal; Macartney embassy reaches China | The Permanent Settlement fixed land revenue forever and created a new landlord class. The Qianlong Emperor told Macartney China had no need of British goods |
| 1793–1798 | Britain invades French Saint-Domingue (Haiti) | Tens of thousands of British troops die, mostly of yellow fever, and Britain withdraws |
| 1795 | Britain takes the Dutch Cape Colony | Handed back in 1803, retaken in 1806 |
| 1796 | Britain takes coastal Ceylon from the Dutch | Crown colony from 1802 |
| 1797 | Naval mutinies at Spithead and the Nore | At the height of the war, sailors strike over pay and conditions |
| 1798 | **Irish Rebellion** of the United Irishmen; Nelson wins the Battle of the Nile | French troops land at Killala in August, too late |
| 1799 | **Fall of Seringapatam; Tipu Sultan killed** | Mysore broken; Arthur Wellesley (later Wellington) gains his first major experience |
| 1800 | Malta taken from the French; Act of Union with Ireland passed | |

## Main timeline (1801–1815)

| Year | What happened | Why it matters |
|---|---|---|
| 1801 | **United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland** formed (1 January) | Ireland's parliament abolished; Catholic emancipation promised and then not delivered |
| 1803 | Second Anglo-Maratha War; victories at Assaye and Delhi | The Mughal Emperor Shah Alam II comes under British "protection" |
| 1803 | Robert Emmet's rising in Dublin | Small, quickly crushed; Emmet hanged |
| 1803 | Settlement of Van Diemen's Land (Tasmania) | |
| 1805 | Battle of Trafalgar | Ends the threat of invasion and secures British naval dominance for a century |
| 1806 | **Vellore Mutiny** (July); Cape retaken; failed invasions of Buenos Aires (1806–1807) | Vellore is a warning sign 50 years before 1857 |
| 1807 | **Abolition of the Slave Trade Act** (25 March) | British ships banned from the trade. Slavery itself continues in the colonies |
| 1808 | Sierra Leone becomes a crown colony; West Africa Squadron starts patrolling against slavers; Rum Rebellion in New South Wales | The officers of the NSW Corps depose Governor William Bligh (of Bounty fame) |
| 1810–1811 | Mauritius and Java taken from France and its Dutch ally | Mauritius kept; Java returned in 1816 |
| 1812–1815 | **War of 1812** with the United States | Washington burned in 1814; British-allied Indigenous leader Tecumseh killed in 1813; ends in a draw |
| 1814 | Treaty of Ghent; Dutch formally cede the Cape | |
| 1814–1816 | Anglo-Nepal (Gurkha) War | Treaty of Sugauli; Gurkhas begin serving in the British Indian Army |
| 1815 | Kandyan Kingdom in Ceylon annexed; **Waterloo (18 June)**; Congress of Vienna | Britain keeps Malta, the Cape, Ceylon, Mauritius, Trinidad, Tobago, St Lucia, the Ionian Islands (protectorate) and Heligoland |

## Meanwhile: the rest of the world (1783–1815)

| Years | Event | Region |
|---|---|---|
| 1787 | US Constitution written | United States |
| 1789 | **French Revolution** begins | France, one year after the First Fleet reached Australia |
| 1791 | **Haitian Revolution** begins in Saint-Domingue | Caribbean. The largest successful slave revolt in history |
| 1793 | Execution of Louis XVI; the Terror | France |
| 1796 | White Lotus Rebellion begins (to 1804) | Qing China starts its long 19th-century decline |
| 1798–1801 | Napoleon's invasion of Egypt | Middle East. Part of the reason was to threaten British India |
| 1803 | Louisiana Purchase | United States |
| 1804 | **Haiti declares independence**; Napoleon crowned emperor | |
| 1804 | Uthman dan Fodio's jihad begins, creating the Sokoto Caliphate | West Africa. Britain conquers it 99 years later |
| 1805–1848 | Muhammad Ali rules and modernises Egypt | Middle East |
| 1807 | United States also bans the import of enslaved people (effective 1808) | |
| 1808 | Napoleon invades Spain; the Spanish-American independence wars begin from 1810 | Latin America; British merchants and volunteers back many of the rebels |
| 1810 | Hidalgo's Grito de Dolores | Mexico |
| 1812 | Napoleon's invasion of Russia | Same year the War of 1812 started |
| 1815 | Eruption of Mount Tambora | Indonesia; leads to the "year without a summer" in 1816 |
| c.1816–1828 | Rise of the Zulu kingdom under Shaka | Southern Africa |

## Resistance: risings, mutinies and wars

| Years | Who | Where | Outcome |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1790–1799 | Tipu Sultan of Mysore | South India | Killed at Seringapatam; Mysore restored to the Wodeyar dynasty under British control |
| 1795–1796 | **Fédon's Rebellion** | Grenada | Free people of colour and enslaved people, inspired by the French Revolution, hold most of the island for over a year |
| 1795–1796 | Second Maroon War (Trelawny Town) | Jamaica | Maroons deported to Nova Scotia and later Sierra Leone |
| 1795–1797 | **Second Carib War** | St Vincent | Garifuna leader Joseph Chatoyer killed; about 5,000 Garifuna deported, survivors taken to Roatán in Honduras |
| 1798 | United Irishmen rising | Ireland | Crushed, with heavy loss of life (often estimated at 10,000 to 30,000 dead) |
| 1799–1805 | Polygar Wars; Pazhassi Raja's revolt | South India | Local chiefs crushed; Pazhassi Raja killed in 1805 |
| 1803–1805 | Marathas (Scindia, Bhonsle, Holkar) | Central and northern India | Defeated, but not yet destroyed |
| 1806 | Vellore Mutiny | South India | Sepoys rise over new rules on dress, beards and caste marks; about 350 mutineers killed when the fort was retaken, and around twenty more formally executed, some blown from cannon |
| 1808 | Rum Rebellion | New South Wales | The only successful armed takeover of government in Australian history |
| 1803–1815 | Kandyan Kingdom | Ceylon | Survives the first British attack (1803); annexed 1815; a major uprising follows in 1817–1818 |
| 1812–1813 | Tecumseh's confederacy (allied with Britain against the US) | Great Lakes | Defeated by the US; a reminder that Indigenous nations used Britain as an ally against settler expansion too |

## Things that happened at the same time

- **1788–1789.** Australia was founded, Hastings was put on trial for misrule in India, and the French Revolution began, in an eighteen-month window.
- **1791–1804.** Haiti's revolution ran alongside Britain's first serious abolition campaign. British troops lost a war in Saint-Domingue in the 1790s while trying to take the colony and its slaves for Britain. The Haitian example terrified slaveholders across the Caribbean and also strengthened abolitionists' argument that slavery was dangerous as well as immoral.
- **1798.** In one year: the Irish rising, Napoleon in Egypt, and Wellesley's arrival in India as Governor-General planning to destroy Tipu. The three are connected, since Tipu had sought French help and the French landed in Ireland.
- **1807.** Britain banned its slave trade; the US did the same weeks later. In the same years, the Sokoto Caliphate was growing in West Africa, Muhammad Ali was taking power in Egypt, and Britain was trying (and failing) to invade Buenos Aires.
- **1815.** Waterloo, the Congress of Vienna, the annexation of Kandy, the Gurkha war and the Tambora eruption all fall in the same year.

- Maya Jasanoff, *Liberty's Exiles: American Loyalists in the Revolutionary World* (2011).
- Robert Hughes, *The Fatal Shore* (1986), on convict Australia.
- Kim Wagner and others on Vellore; for a general account see Encyclopaedia Britannica, "Vellore Mutiny".
- Thomas Bartlett, *Ireland: A History* (2010), on 1798 and the Union.
- UK Parliament, "The Abolition of the Slave Trade Act 1807": https://www.parliament.uk
- **Flag:** The 1798 death toll in Ireland is a rough range used in many textbooks; there is no firm figure. British losses in Saint-Domingue (often given as 40,000 or more dead from disease across the Caribbean campaigns of the 1790s) also vary widely by source and by which islands are counted. Loyalist emigration figures are estimates. Vellore casualty and execution figures differ between contemporary reports.
